routes.title: 🏙️ Recognize objects in a 3D scene
routes.summary: Point features → semantic labels → separate object instances
routes.goal: Labeling points as 'chair' doesn't tell you how many chairs there are. Start with point-cloud features, then look at the methods that separate individual objects.

steps.label: Start with what a point feature remembers
steps.focus: PointNet summarizes a whole set; PointNet++ brings local neighborhoods back into the representation.

steps.label: See how the backbone scales up
steps.focus: Compare Point Transformer V3's serialized points with volumetric patch tokens and global attention.

steps.label: Turn labels into individual objects
steps.focus: Watch point features become semantic, instance, and panoptic predictions rather than one class label per point.

steps.label: Ask what survives a new dataset
steps.focus: Contrast transferred 2D features with training across multiple 3D datasets, then ask what was actually held out.

routes.try_it: Take a kitchen scan and mark what a semantic map, an instance map, and a panoptic map would each preserve.

routes.title: 🗣️ Find objects and parts using language
routes.summary: Open vocabulary → scene relations → actionable parts
routes.goal: Finding a fridge and opening it are different jobs. Start with text queries, then see how methods locate doors, handles, and other parts a robot can use.

steps.label: Query a map with text
steps.focus: See how visual-language features answer queries that a fixed category list cannot anticipate.

steps.label: Find the particular object being described
steps.focus: Compare how 2D observations and 3D proposals turn an open-vocabulary query into an object mask.

steps.label: Understand descriptions such as “the one on the left”
steps.focus: Put referring-expression localization beside a scene graph: one finds an object, the other keeps relations available for planning.

steps.label: Find the door or handle needed for the task
steps.focus: Follow task descriptions and affordances down to actionable parts, part poses, and candidate interaction regions.

routes.try_it: Compare the regions needed for 'find the refrigerator' and 'open the refrigerator': object, door, handle, and action space.

routes.title: 🏗️ Reconstruct a room from photos or video
routes.summary: Camera geometry → neural representations → learned geometry → online mapping
routes.goal: Do you need a new camera view, a surface model, or a map that updates as you move? That choice matters when you pick a reconstruction method.

steps.label: Recover cameras and geometry
steps.focus: Compare camera-and-sparse-structure recovery from images with globally consistent RGB-D surface fusion.

steps.label: Represent scene appearance
steps.focus: Contrast a continuous radiance field with explicit Gaussians, keeping rendering quality separate from surface geometry.

steps.label: Predict geometry directly
steps.focus: Study feed-forward point maps, camera recovery, depth, and how much multi-view consistency is built in.

steps.label: Map an ongoing observation stream
steps.focus: Compare implicit and Gaussian maps as both map and camera pose are updated during a stream.

steps.label: Handle a changing scene
steps.focus: Separate estimating changing geometry and cameras from merely rendering a dynamic scene.

routes.try_it: For one captured room, list which methods need depth, camera poses, multiple views, or scene-specific optimization, and which outputs support rendering or geometry queries.

routes.title: 🌍 Generate a 3D environment
routes.summary: Layouts → visual worlds → procedural environments → simulation tasks
routes.goal: Start by arranging furniture, then look at how methods build whole rooms and worlds. If a robot needs to use the result, there's more to check than how it looks.

steps.label: Place objects before rendering them
steps.focus: Compare autoregressive layout prediction with diffusion over scene configurations.

steps.label: Turn a room request into spatial constraints
steps.focus: Ask whether the text becomes explicit object relations and layout constraints, or only a loose conditioning signal.

steps.label: Build a world from a prompt or image
steps.focus: Contrast a generated textured room mesh with interactive scene expansion from an image.

steps.label: Sample a training world procedurally
steps.focus: Compare interactive indoor-house sampling with procedural natural-world geometry and materials.

steps.label: Give generation a task and a simulator
steps.focus: Read for task-driven scene construction and the interface between generated environments and agent training.

routes.try_it: Give one room description to a layout generator, a visual scene generator, and a simulator generator. Write down what each returns and what a robot would still be missing.

routes.title: ⚙️ Work out how doors and drawers move
routes.summary: Parts → joints and pose → tracking → scene articulation
routes.goal: A robot needs to know which side a door hinges on and which way a drawer slides. Read about finding movable parts, estimating motion, and tracking their state.

steps.label: Separate a moving part from its motion
steps.focus: Compare a motion-part decomposition with category-level pose and canonical part coordinates: which variables make the joint explicit?

steps.label: Keep track of a moving joint over time
steps.focus: Study how previous-frame estimates support online per-part pose tracking.

steps.label: Infer opening parts from one image
steps.focus: Follow openable-part detection and axis estimation from single-object to multi-object images.

steps.label: Carry articulation into a cluttered room
steps.focus: Examine scene-level parts, handles, connectivity, and articulation predictions.

routes.try_it: For one door and one drawer, write the part mask, joint type, axis, origin, and state a robot would need before acting.

routes.title: 🧩 Rebuild an object with moving parts
routes.summary: Observations → geometry and motion → executable models
routes.goal: A reconstructed cabinet may look right but still have no doors that open. Here's how methods recover parts and joints so the model can move in a simulator.

steps.label: Use state changes as evidence
steps.focus: Compare before/after interaction observations with multi-view capture in two states: what becomes observable only after motion?

steps.label: Recover parts and joints from video
steps.focus: Compare how the methods recover shape, separate moving parts, and estimate joints from a monocular video.

steps.label: Write the result into an executable model
steps.focus: Compare reconstructed parts and articulation code with single-image, mesh-based URDF prediction.

steps.label: Add motion to a static asset
steps.focus: Inspect part detection, motion inference, hidden-geometry completion, and scene assembly.

routes.try_it: Make a small input/output table: single image, two states, video, or static mesh in; geometry, joints, and executable assets out.

routes.title: 🛠️ Generate objects with joints
routes.summary: Part graphs → conditional generation → asset programs
routes.goal: Generating a cabinet with working doors means producing more than its shape. Look at how models generate parts, connections, and motion parameters together.

steps.label: Write down the part graph first
steps.focus: Read for graph representations, part geometry, motion parameters, and structural constraints.

steps.label: Condition the graph on evidence or language
steps.focus: Compare physical guidance and partial observations with text-conditioned tree generation; note which constraint fixes which ambiguity.

steps.label: Infer a movable asset from one view
steps.focus: Compare plausible geometry and kinematics inferred from one image.

steps.label: Generate the program behind the asset
steps.focus: Trace how language/vision models produce programs defining parts, joints, and simulator assets.

routes.try_it: Draw two plausible models of the same closed cabinet. What does the image settle, and what must the generator invent?

routes.title: 🧭 Help an agent find its way
routes.summary: Spatial maps → semantic goals → language instructions → lifelong navigation
routes.goal: The target may be out of sight, and the instruction may be vague. See how maps, exploration, and memory help an agent decide where to go.

steps.label: Put language features on a map
steps.focus: See how visual-language features are fused into a spatial map that can name both a goal and an obstacle.

steps.label: Choose where to look next
steps.focus: Ask how frontier exploration changes once the robot can recognize a semantic goal from its current view.

steps.label: Turn route language into landmarks
steps.focus: Trace a named landmark from language to visual grounding and then to the navigation controller.

steps.label: Test whether memory helps after the first goal
steps.focus: Compare one-off route following with repeated category, image, and language goals that reward retaining scene memory.

routes.try_it: For “find the mug near the sofa,” separate the target description, map state, next exploration move, and memory carried over from earlier goals.

routes.title: 💡 Let an agent explore and answer questions
routes.summary: Gather observations → ground questions → reason → plan
routes.goal: To answer 'what is on the table?', an agent may need to go and look. This route covers gathering observations, reasoning about the scene, and planning what to do next.

steps.label: Decide what evidence the question needs
steps.focus: Compare navigating to gather fresh evidence with answering from episodic memory and active exploration.

steps.label: Give a language model a scene to reason over
steps.focus: Study the interface between 3D scene features and language-based questions, dialogue, and plans.

steps.label: Reuse scene features across tasks
steps.focus: Compare 3D vision-language-action instruction tuning with language models that receive continuous visual and robot-state inputs.

steps.label: Reject a plan that cannot be executed
steps.focus: Contrast controller-grounded plans with skill selection constrained by learned feasibility; where can each stop a bad action?

routes.try_it: Ask “what is on the kitchen table?” from remembered images, then decide what missing evidence would justify one more action.

routes.title: 🦾 Get a robot to grasp, push, or open
routes.summary: Affordances → motion planning → feedback → mobile manipulation
routes.goal: Where should the robot make contact, which way should it move, and what should it do if that fails? Read about affordances, motion estimates, and feedback from touch.

steps.label: Choose a contact region
steps.focus: Compare actionability predictions with affordances that explicitly account for occlusion and robot position.

steps.label: Represent how the object can move
steps.focus: Contrast dense motion fields with articulation models and adaptive joint estimation before choosing a trajectory.

steps.label: Let contact revise the motion hypothesis
steps.focus: Use observation history for uncertain motion hypotheses, then see how tactile feedback changes the controller.

steps.label: Move the base as well as the arm
steps.focus: See how perception, base navigation, whole-body planning, grasping, and adaptation have to agree at a real site.

routes.try_it: Trace one failed door-opening attempt: what would a new camera view, contact measurement, or base move change?

routes.title: 🤖 Understand general-purpose robot policies
routes.summary: Action learning → vision-language-action → planning and recovery
routes.goal: Some models predict actions directly; others make a language plan first. Compare these approaches and the scene information they need during a task.

steps.label: Sample actions from demonstrations
steps.focus: See how conditional action diffusion uses visual input and receding-horizon execution rather than one fixed trajectory.

steps.label: Add language to the action model
steps.focus: Compare flow-matching action experts with co-training across robot and semantic data.

steps.label: Compare two open policy families
steps.focus: Contrast a vision-language-action model with a transformer diffusion policy across embodiments and adaptation settings.

steps.label: Check language plans against the scene
steps.focus: Compare affordance-value-guided skill selection with programs that build spatial 3D value maps.

steps.label: Recover after a failed interaction
steps.focus: Track how semantic, actionable parts become an executable policy and a feedback-driven retry.

routes.try_it: For “put the cup in the cabinet,” separate task planning, scene grounding, contact selection, and action execution.

routes.title: 📊 Pick a dataset and decide what to measure
routes.summary: Scene labels → functional annotations → simulation → household tasks
routes.goal: Scene segmentation and opening a cabinet need different data and different tests. Start with the ability you want to measure, then choose a benchmark that can test it.

steps.label: Choose the scene evidence you need
steps.focus: Compare high-fidelity scene capture with long-tail semantic and instance-label coverage; neither one alone defines the task.

steps.label: Add labels for function and motion
steps.focus: Compare mobility annotations, task-grounded functional regions, and executable articulated scene structure.

steps.label: Move from annotations to interactive assets
steps.focus: Compare physics-based part interaction with procedurally generated articulated-object data.

steps.label: Check what a manipulation score really measures
steps.focus: Read the robot interface, observations, demonstrations, and split before comparing a manipulation score.

steps.label: Test long-horizon household behavior
steps.focus: Compare compositional kitchen-task generalization with long-horizon activity that changes object state.

steps.label: Separate answering, doing, and asking
steps.focus: Keep question-answering accuracy, household task completion, and dialogue-conditioned interaction as separate evidence.

routes.try_it: Choose one segmentation benchmark and one cabinet-opening benchmark; write down their inputs, success metric, and withheld split.
